html:
Kashgar is an oasis city at the western edge of the Tarim Basin in Xinjiang, western China, at the foot of the Pamir and Tian Shan mountains. For over 2,000 years it was a crossroads of the Silk Road, where routes around the Taklamakan Desert met the passes west to Fergana and Samarkand and south to India.

In early centuries it was a Buddhist oasis kingdom, drawn by turns under Chinese and steppe control. Han generals reached it in the first century CE, soon after the Silk Road opened, and the Tang held it as a garrison town in the 600s and 700s.

In the 900s it became a seat of the Kara-Khanids, the first Turkic dynasty to accept Islam, after Satuq Bughra Khan turned Muslim. Kashgar grew into a centre of Turkic Muslim learning. Yusuf of Balasagun presented the Kutadgu Bilig to its ruler in 1069, and Mahmud al-Kashgari wrote the first dictionary of the Turkic languages.

Mongols, Chagatai khans and local Muslim rulers followed. The Qing conquered it in 1759. In 1865 Yaqub Beg made it the capital of a short-lived state, and in the late 1800s Britain and Russia kept consulates there to watch each other. It remains a mainly Uyghur city, centred on the Id Kah Mosque. The Karakoram Highway now links it to Pakistan.
